title: Vote the person, not the issues
subtitle: Plus a few thoughts on spy scandals
contentHtml:

Most intellectuals believe that voters should ignore personal characteristics and “vote the issues”. That may be true in some cases, but I suspect it is much less true than many highly political people assume. New York mayor Zohran Mamdani and Chicago mayor Brandon Johnson have similar (left wing) ideologies. But I expect Mamdani to be more successful for reasons that have nothing to do with ideology—he’s much more capable.

In many cases it’s a close call, where it is difficult to determine how much weight to put on integrity and competence and how much weight to put on policy views. Unlike many libertarians, I was never completely on the Milei bandwagon. I supported his economic policy proposals, but had grave doubts about his character. Nonetheless, I probably would have held my nose and voted for him.

At first, it looked like things were going well. But in the long run character always wins out, and now we have this (from The Economist):

Subsequently, on September 3rd, Mr Milei, flanked by his cabinet, declared publicly that “winds of change” would favour Argentina’s claim to the islands. It was a reference to comments made earlier the same day by Donald Trump, in which he seemed to indicate that he would not support Britain in a dispute over the islands. Mr Milei also hinted that Argentina would impose sanctions on any companies that tried to develop oil resources in the Falklands.

Given Trump’s refusal to condemn Putin, and his own desire to conquer Greenland, is there much doubt as to where Trump’s preferences lie regarding the Falklands?

I still believe that Milei might succeed, but I’d have more confidence if he were not so impulsive.

Unlike Milei, Trump is not a close call. Apart from illegal immigration, he has abandoned almost every political position that he took as a candidate. Here are just a few examples:

  1. Promises to refrain from neoconservative policies in the Middle East

  2. Promises to reduce the national debt

  3. Promises to end the (woke) romanticizing of oppressed minority groups

  4. Promises to end cancel culture

  5. Promises to end lawfare

  6. Promises to oppose socialism

  7. Promises to end corruption, to “drain the swamp”.

  8. Promises to end the sloppy handling of national security secrets

  9. Promises to boost high-skilled immigration

  10. Promises to reduce regulatory barriers to energy production

Note that in almost every case, these reversals were predictable if you assumed that policy reflected character, not political platforms. Regarding the ten issues cited above:

  1. Trump has an aggressive personality. He likes to pick fights.

  2. Trump has always liked debt. He has a “one marshmallow” personality. “Apres moi, le deluge.”

  3. Trump romanticizes right-wing “victims”, such as Afrikaner farmers, or conservative thugs that beat up cops. Right-wing wokism.

  4. Trump likes to silence people that criticize him.

  5. Trump likes to use his power to seek revenge against those who displeased him.

  6. Trump likes to do things; laissez-faire economics is not a part of his personality.

  7. Trump is a dishonest person, why would he oppose corruption?

  8. Trump is both arrogant and sloppy, why would he be careful with national security secrets?

  9. Trump doesn’t like foreigners that don’t look like Norwegian supermodels. Most high skilled immigrants are non-white

  10. Trump hates windmills and solar farms—why would he deregulate energy production?

The bigger the personality flaws, the more likely it is that they will eventually show up in policy failures. If you “vote the issues” for a candidate that lacks a suitable character for higher office, you will almost always end up being disappointed. No one should be surprised by Trump’s support for price controls, inflationary monetary policy, bans on Chinese cars, creating state-owned enterprises, wars in the Middle East, etc.

Admittedly, the argument for “voting the issues” becomes stronger for non-executive positions, such as senator and congressman. But consider the fact that only seven GOP senators voted to convict Trump after January 6. If there had been 17 GOP senators with integrity, then we would have a different president today (DeSantis?)

Here’s the Financial Times, discussing Japan’s new Prime Minister:

Her personal ideal is the indefatigable Margaret Thatcher, a notoriously light sleeper who trounced patricians and, supporters say, injected dynamism into an intransigent economy through sheer force of will.

Thatcher took unpopular positions, giving the UK some painful but needed medicine. In contrast, Takaichi seems attached to the sort of populist policies that have not worked in other places:

Other limitations on Takaichi’s plans to “aggressively hit the growth switch” have also become more visible.

Where she has been most radical in the commitment to fight inflation, by capping petrol prices and pushing a plan to cut consumption tax on food from 8 per cent to 1 per cent, she has drawn as much scepticism for the fiscal risk as support for the potential relief. . . .

Older voters fret that her growth-driven spending plans threaten the foundation of their single biggest concern: the health of Japan’s social security system.

There are, to some critics, obvious fragilities in Takaichi’s self-isolated governance style and, to others, outright errors of judgment on tax cuts, dramatically tighter immigration rules and an industrial policy that involves funnelling ¥370tn ($2.3tn) of public and private sector investment into 17 sectors of the economy.

I hope I’m wrong, but I do not see her as another Thatcher. Populism is the easy way out in the short run, but very destructive in the long run.

In my view, the “vote the issues” argument was stronger in the 20th century, when a certain level of integrity was a given in American politics, and the capitalism vs. socialism debate was still unresolved. Today, a mostly capitalist mixed economy is the only plausible economic system, and public policy is primarily about making the system work more efficiently and fairly. For that you need people with integrity, not corrupt ideologues.

PS. This recent article caught my eye:

New court, same losing argument.

The federal Department of Transportation continues to insist that the president and his agencies can do whatever they want, whenever they want, as the Trump administration tries without success to destroy congestion pricing in New York City.

In June, U.S. DOT appealed Judge Lewis Liman’s March decision in favor of the MTA, which sued the federal government over President Trump’s attempt to kill the Manhattan toll. In their brief, the feds asked court, not for the first time, to endorse the idea that Trump’s whims, rather that the law, have the final say over his government’s actions.

This is the sort of idiotic action that reflects personality, not ideology. No other GOP president would have done this.

PPS. Trump likes bullies. Here is the National Review:

Jim Geraghty noted this week that he faced pushback for saying in 2025 that America had “effectively switched sides in the Russia-Ukraine War.” Since then,

“we’ve seen the Trump administration roll out the red carpet (literally) for Vladimir Putin in Alaska, invite Putin to the G-20 summit, and invite other Russian officials to a separate G-20 meeting. President Trump has also declared that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky should be replaced, contradicted his own cabinet about Russia’s help to Iran, downplayed an obvious and ongoing series of Russian hybrid warfare attacks against our European NATO allies, and turned down offers of Ukrainian assistance with drone production.”

And yet, as much as those developments reinforce the impression that we are, in fact, on the wrong side, the relationship between America and Ukraine worsens still. It may soon hit a breaking point.

PPPS. Off topic: Since the Jensen Huang scandal is in the news, I thought I’d offer a few comments. Long time readers know that I believe that human “cloak and dagger” spying is greatly overrated. I won’t say it has zero value, but unlike spy satellites (which are quite useful), the importance of human spying is exaggerated by Hollywood films. I can think of two possible objectives for the Chinese spy—getting valuable technical secrets and persuading Huang to advocate for chip exports to China. But Huang already favored those exports for straightforward financial reasons, and it would probably be easier to get technical secrets by having a Chinese engineer work within Nvidia. I doubt there were candlelight dinners where the seductive spy purred “tell me more about the technical specs of your newest Blackwell chip.”

In any case, this particular case of spying clearly ended up being a big net negative for China. It makes it much harder for Nvidia to advocate for chip exports to China, as people will naturally tend to recall the spying scandal and thus become even more skeptical of Nvidia’s position. China would be better off if Huang were still in charge and there had been no scandal.

In the real world, spying that has value is too boring for even a le Carré novel. It’s things like spy satellites and ordinary Chinese engineers getting technical information by working within American firms. Yawn.

And finally, this made me smile:

"I just know Jensen very well," added Trump. "I just think he's a very honorable man."

Takes one to know one?
